name: Recognizing governments that took power by force in Latin America, 1865–1980
introductionText: What FRUS answers directly: for more than a century the Department of State recognized a Latin American government that had seized power once it controlled the machinery of the state without substantial resistance, had at least the acquiescence of its people, and was able and willing to meet the country's international obligations (FRUS 1900, Document 530; 1930, Volume I, Document 375; 1948, Volume IX, Document 7; 1969–1976, Volume E–11, Part 2, Document 34). Around that test it added demands: constitutional ratification of the new order (Seward in the 1860s, Wilson after 1913, and the Central American treaty rule of 1923–1934); specific concessions bargained for before recognition (Mexico 1877 and 1921–1923, the Dominican Republic 1903, Haiti 1914); prior consultation with the other American republics and action against the Axis (1943–1945); and, after 1948, assurances on obligations, elections, civil liberties and communism, while holding that recognition implied no approval. By the 1970s it stopped speaking of recognition and decided only whether relations continued. The set behind this is about 2,100 documents in 115 of the 553 volumes; the 52 documents here carry the argument (44 from that set, 8 reached by reading its chapters and cross-references). Where FRUS points for the rest: the printed documents came overwhelmingly from the Department's Central Decimal File in Record Group 59 (the country 'Political affairs' and 'Government' classes), from 1963 the Subject-Numeric file POL 16 ('Independence. Recognition.'), office files such as the Policy Planning Staff Chronological Files (Lot 64 D 563) and the Kennedy and Johnson National Security Files; the editors' footnotes cite further unprinted decimal-file folders and lots such as the Office of Central American and Panamanian Affairs files (Lot 63 D 127) and the Rubottom–Mann files (Lot 62 D 418). What this request cannot get from FRUS: the public statements that announced the shifts (Acheson 1949, Mann 1964, Senate Resolution 205 of 1969) are cited, not printed; the Latin American governments' own deliberations appear only as U.S. diplomats reported them; the 1980s are almost absent (one partial South America volume); and before 1910 FRUS gives no source notes, so the nineteenth-century files can only be inferred from the despatch series.

headings.F1: 1. One working test throughout: control, consent, and the country's obligations
headings.F2: 2. Constitutional origin as the test: Seward, Wilson, and the Central American treaty rule
headings.F3: 3. Recognition as a price: concessions demanded before recognition (1877–1923)
headings.F4: 4. Wartime: the hemisphere consults, and the test is the war (1943–1945)
headings.F5: 5. After Bogotá: recognition implies no approval, and withholding it is a feeble weapon (1948–1960)
headings.F6: 6. Elections and civil liberties, then the retreat from recognition (1961–1980)

prose.F1: These documents state the standing test in the Department's own words, from Fish's handling of Díaz in 1877 to Ambassador Hill's statement to the Argentine military in 1976: effective control without substantial resistance, the acquiescence or support of the people, and the ability and willingness to meet international obligations. Roosevelt's Cuban criteria of 1933 and the Legal Adviser's 1938 ruling on self-coups show how the test was read at the edges.
prose.F2: This thread follows the periods in which Washington demanded that a government installed by force be ratified by its people through constitutional means: Seward's Peru instructions of 1865–1868, Wilson's 1913 statement and the terms put to Huerta, the refusal to recognize Tinoco, and the Central American treaty rule from 1907 and 1923 through Martínez's recognition in 1934 and the formal abandonment in 1936.
prose.F3: These documents show recognition withheld until a new government agreed to specific terms: border policing from Díaz, a pledge to honor prior engagements in the Dominican Republic, a customs convention and other settlements from Haiti, and a property-rights treaty and claims conventions from Obregón's Mexico.
prose.F4: During the Second World War the United States tied recognition to the war: Resolution XXII required prior consultation among the American republics, and the Bolivian and Argentine regimes were held to concrete measures against the Axis before recognition. These documents follow that procedure from December 1943 to April 1945.
prose.F5: The Policy Planning Staff paper of March 1948 and the Bogotá resolution recast recognition as implying no approval; Kennan's and Daniels's memoranda judged non-recognition a feeble sanction. The 1949–1960 cases show the assurances still sought: international obligations, private capital, anti-communism and elections.
prose.F6: Under Kennedy the United States withheld recognition to press juntas toward elections and civil liberties (Peru 1962; the Dominican Republic and Honduras 1963) and then judged the leverage spent; under Johnson it sought the usual assurances without insisting on an election date; from 1968 officials proposed that a coup should change the level of relations rather than end them, and by 1973 the Department avoided the word recognition altogether.

closingHeading: Threads this run could not follow
closingProse: Agent note, run r10, 2026-10-25: not followed here — (1) the public texts of Acheson's 19 September 1949 statement, Mann's June 1964 Notre Dame speech and Senate Resolution 205 (1969), which the documents cite but FRUS does not print (Department of State Bulletin; Congressional Record); (2) the Latin American foreign ministries' side of each decision, visible here only through U.S. reporting; (3) the Uruguayan Larreta proposal of 1945 and the Venezuelan Betancourt position of the 1960s, which the documents mention; (4) the Resolution XXVI consultation procedure of 1965 in its own text; (5) the 1980s, for which the corpus holds only a partial South America volume; (6) the unprinted decimal-file folders and lots named in the archival sources below, which hold the documents the editors chose not to print.
